key_terms.meaning: No device working in a cycle can take heat from one reservoir and convert it fully into work; some heat must always be rejected to a colder sink.
No device working in a cycle can move heat from a cold body to a hot body with zero work input.
A cyclic device that absorbs Q_H from a hot reservoir at T_H, rejects Q_C to a cold reservoir at T_C, and delivers W = Q_H − Q_C.
A cyclic device that takes Q_C from a cold space and dumps Q_H = Q_C + W to the surroundings using work W.
A refrigerator whose useful output is the heat Q_H delivered to the hot space; COP_HP = Q_H/W = COP_R + 1.
Useful heat moved divided by work input: COP_R = Q_C/W for a refrigerator, COP_HP = Q_H/W for a heat pump.
A fully reversible cycle of two isothermal and two adiabatic steps between T_H and T_C; efficiency η = 1 − T_C/T_H.
No cycle between two fixed reservoirs beats a reversible one, and all reversible cycles between them have the same efficiency; η depends only on T_H and T_C.
A scale fixed only by reversible heat ratios, T_C/T_H = Q_C/Q_H, independent of the working fluid.
State function S with dS = δQ_rev/T for a reversible path; for a real path ΔS > ∫δQ/T. Units J/K.
For any cycle, ∮δQ/T ≤ 0; the equality holds only when the cycle is fully reversible.
S_gen is the entropy created by irreversibility inside a process; S_gen ≥ 0, and S_gen = 0 only for a reversible process.
A perfect crystal at 0 K has zero entropy; entropy changes vanish as T → 0, so absolute entropies can be tabulated.
Work destroyed by irreversibility, W_lost = T₀ S_gen, where T₀ is the surroundings temperature in K.
The practical steam power cycle: pump, boiler, turbine, condenser, with efficiency η = (W_T − W_P)/Q_in.
Bleeding part of the steam from the turbine to preheat boiler feed water, raising the mean temperature of heat addition and hence η.
Temperature change on throttling at constant enthalpy; μ_JT = (∂T/∂P)_H is positive below the inversion temperature, so the gas cools.
Liquefaction cycle that cools the gas in a counter-current heat exchanger and expands part of it in an engine to make work, giving a higher liquid yield than simple throttling.
One specific microscopic arrangement of the molecules of a system; a macrostate is a set of microstates with the same measured properties.
Entropy still present at 0 K when a crystal is not perfect, for example because molecules freeze in random orientations.

takeaways: The second law is a statement about direction: work can turn completely into heat, but heat cannot turn completely into work in a cycle.
A heat engine, a refrigerator and a heat pump are the same energy balance read in three different directions.
The Carnot efficiency 1 − T_C/T_H is a ceiling set only by reservoir temperatures, not by the fluid or the machine.
Entropy is a state function; ΔS = ∫δQ_rev/T over any convenient reversible path between the same two states.
The Clausius inequality ∮δQ/T ≤ 0 is the seed from which the whole entropy concept grows.
For a control volume, entropy carried in by flow and heat plus entropy generated equals entropy carried out plus accumulation.
Every real process destroys work equal to T₀ S_gen, and that gap is what a second-law (exergy) analysis measures.
Real power plants and refrigerators are engineered by pushing their cycles closer to the reversible ideal — reheat, regeneration, and careful choice of boiler, condenser and evaporator pressures.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for a statement, a labelled sketch and a derivation, so show the equivalence of the two second-law statements and derive efficiency or COP from first principles before plugging in numbers.

bank.q: State the Kelvin–Planck and the Clausius statements of the second law and show that each one implies the other.
outline: Write both statements exactly, naming the reservoirs and the cycle.
Assume a Kelvin–Planck violator, couple it to a reversible refrigerator, and show heat is pumped from cold to hot with no work — a Clausius violation.
Assume a Clausius violator, couple it to a reversible heat engine, and show a single reservoir driving a cycle to give work — a Kelvin–Planck violation.
Conclude both statements are equivalent forms of the same law.

bank.q: Define entropy as a state function. Show that ∫δQ_rev/T between two states is independent of the reversible path.
outline: Show that ∮δQ_rev/T = 0 for a reversible cycle using the Carnot result Q_C/Q_H = T_C/T_H.
Split a reversible cycle into two paths A and B between states 1 and 2.
Conclude that ∫δQ_rev/T is the same along A and B, so dS = δQ_rev/T is exact.
State that S is a property, and compare with the path functions Q and W.

bank.q: State the third law of thermodynamics and explain why absolute entropies can be tabulated and why residual entropy can still appear at 0 K.
outline: Perfect crystal at 0 K has one microstate, so S = 0.
Entropy integrals ∫(C_p/T)dT are finite from 0 K upward, so a reference zero is usable.
Real crystals may freeze in disordered orientations (CO, glassy solids), leaving residual entropy.
Mention that the third law lets tables report absolute S values rather than differences.

bank.q: Explain the microscopic meaning of entropy using S = k_B ln Ω, with the example of gas molecules in two halves of a box.
outline: Define microstate and macrostate; k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K.
Number of ways to place N molecules so that n are in one half: Ω = N!/[n!(N−n)!].
All-in-one-half has Ω = 1, S = 0; even split has the largest Ω and the largest S.
This explains why gas expands to fill both halves — the system drifts to the most probable macrostate.

bank.q: A Carnot engine works between 800 K and 300 K and receives 500 kJ from the hot reservoir. Find the efficiency, the work output and the heat rejected. Then find the COP of a Carnot refrigerator working between the same two temperatures.
outline: COP_HP = COP_R + 1 = 1.6; keep units kJ and note temperatures must be in K.

bank.q: Calculate the entropy change when 2 kg of water is heated from 300 K to 350 K at constant pressure given c_p = 4.18 kJ/(kg·K), and when the same water is frozen at 273 K with latent heat 334 kJ/kg.
outline: Heating: ΔS = m c_p ln(T₂/T₁) = 2 × 4.18 × ln(350/300) = 1.29 kJ/K.
State clearly that the path chosen must be reversible, e.g. a series of reversible heat additions.
Sign convention and units kJ/K throughout.

bank.q: Steam enters an insulated turbine at 4 MPa and 500 °C and leaves at 10 kPa with a quality of 0.90. Take surroundings at 298 K. Find the entropy generated per kg of steam and the lost work.
outline: Energy balance for the adiabatic turbine: w = h₁ − h₂ from steam tables.
Entropy balance: s₂ − s₁ = s_gen/q, so s_gen = s₂ − s₁ per kg.
Compute s₂ = s_f + x s_fg at 10 kPa.
Lost work = T₀ s_gen with T₀ = 298 K; units kJ/kg.

bank.q: An ideal Rankine cycle operates between boiler pressure 10 MPa and condenser pressure 10 kPa. Sketch the cycle on T–s coordinates and compute its thermal efficiency. Then explain how reheat changes the answer.
outline: Four steps: pump, boiler, turbine, condenser; sketch the dome and the four lines.
η = (w_T − w_P)/q_in, with q_in = h₃ − h₂ and pump work v(P₂ − P₁).
Use saturated liquid at condenser pressure for state 1 and saturated or superheated steam at state 3.
Reheat: expand to an intermediate pressure, reheat at constant pressure, expand again — raises the mean temperature of heat addition and reduces turbine wetness.

bank.q: A vapour-compression refrigerator uses R-134a between evaporator at −10 °C and condenser at 40 °C. Compute the COP for the ideal cycle and explain why the real COP is lower.
outline: Ideal cycle: isentropic compression, condensation, throttling to evaporator, evaporation.
COP = (h₁ − h₄)/[(h₂ − h₁)] using saturation and superheat tables.
Real losses: throttling is irreversible, compressor is not isentropic, pressure drops and heat leaks.
Compare with Carnot COP between the same temperatures to show the gap.

bank.q: Two streams of water, 1 kg/s at 350 K and 1 kg/s at 290 K, are mixed adiabatically in a steady mixer. Calculate the entropy generated and the lost work at T₀ = 290 K, and comment on how the answer would change if the streams were brought together through a reversible heat engine.
outline: Energy balance gives the outlet temperature ≈ 320 K.
ΔS_total = m[c_p ln(320/350)] + m[c_p ln(320/290)], evaluated for each stream, plus no heat term.
S_gen > 0 confirms mixing is irreversible; lost work = T₀ S_gen.
With a reversible engine between the streams, some of the temperature difference is converted to work and S_gen falls to zero.

bank.q: A salesman claims a cyclic device that takes 100 kW of heat from a reservoir at 500 K, rejects heat at 300 K and delivers 60 kW of work. Check the claim using the first law and the second law.
outline: First law: Q_C = 100 − 60 = 40 kW, so the energy balance itself is satisfied.
Carnot limit: η_max = 1 − 300/500 = 0.40, so maximum work is 40 kW.
Alternatively check ΔS of the reservoirs: −100/500 + 40/300 = −0.067 kW/K < 0, impossible.
Conclude the claim violates the second law; a real device must have even lower work output.

bank.q: Compare the Carnot and Rankine cycles for steam power generation. Explain why practical plants do not use the Carnot cycle and how superheat, reheat and regeneration each improve performance.
outline: Carnot cycle needs two-phase compression in the pump, which is impractical; the turbine would run in the wet region.
Rankine uses complete condensation and a cheap liquid pump.
Superheat raises the average temperature of heat addition and dries the turbine exhaust.
Reheat limits exhaust wetness and adds work at high temperature; regeneration raises feed-water temperature and lowers boiler heat input.
Evaluate: each modification moves the real cycle closer to the reversible ceiling between the same source and sink.

bank.q: Explain the Linde and Claude cycles for liquefaction. Why does the Claude cycle give a higher liquid yield, and what role does the Joule–Thomson coefficient play?
outline: Linde: simple throttling after counter-current cooling; yield depends on μ_JT being positive, that is, working below the inversion temperature.
Claude: part of the gas is expanded in an engine doing work, so it cools more and needs no throttling for that portion.
Claude recovers work and reaches lower temperatures, so the fraction liquefied per unit compression work is larger.
Discuss why hydrogen and helium need pre-cooling before throttling (negative μ_JT at room temperature).

bank.q: Define second-law (exergy) efficiency for a steady-flow device and use the entropy balance to discuss where irreversibility arises in a heat exchanger and in a throttling valve.
outline: Entropy balance: Σṁ_in s_in + Σ(Q̇/T) + Ṡ_gen = Σṁ_out s_out for steady state.
Second-law efficiency = ideal work / actual work (or the reverse for work-consuming devices).
Heat exchanger: irreversibility comes from finite temperature difference across the wall, S_gen = ṁ_h Δs_h + ṁ_c Δs_c.
Throttling: h constant, s rises, S_gen > 0, all potential work destroyed; no work recovered.

glossary.def: A body large enough that taking or giving heat does not change its temperature.
Work output divided by heat input of a heat engine, η = W/Q_H.
An ideal process whose direction can be reversed by an infinitesimal change, leaving no trace on the surroundings.
Any effect such as friction, unrestrained expansion or finite-temperature heat transfer that makes a process non-reversible and creates entropy.
A process of constant entropy, the ideal limit for an adiabatic reversible turbine or compressor.
Flow through a restriction with no work and negligible heat transfer, so enthalpy stays constant and pressure falls.
Liquefaction cycle that cools the gas in a counter-current exchanger and then expands it through a throttle valve.
μ_JT = (∂T/∂P)_H; positive means the gas cools on throttling.
Temperature at which μ_JT changes sign; above it a gas warms on throttling.
Entropy measured from the third-law zero at 0 K, as listed in steam and property tables.
The measured, macroscopic description of a system (P, V, T, n) that many microstates can produce.
k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, the entropy per unit of ln Ω.
The work a process would need or deliver if it were fully reversible, W_ideal = W_actual − W_lost.
Ratio of actual performance to the best reversible performance under the same conditions.
A fixed region in space with mass and energy crossing its boundary; used for turbines, compressors and heat exchangers.
Condition where properties inside the control volume do not change with time, so accumulation terms vanish.
Heat exchanger in a power plant that adds Q_in to pressurised water to make steam.
Heat exchanger that rejects Q_out and condenses turbine exhaust back to liquid.
Heating steam above its saturation temperature at the same pressure.
The cold-side heat exchanger of a refrigerator where the refrigerant boils and absorbs Q_C.
∮δQ/T ≤ 0 for any thermodynamic cycle.
An isentropic process, drawn as a vertical line on T–s coordinates.
Accounting statement: entropy in by flow and heat, plus generated entropy, equals entropy out plus accumulation.
